_about: Every correction the user makes becomes a case here, and approved text becomes a pass case. Cases with piece 'house-rules' are taken from the house rules' own examples, not from a correction: they calibrate the reviewer but do not count toward its minimum of the user's own cases. expect: error (test_check_text.py must flag it, with 'contains' in the message), pass (no errors), review (only a reader or the AI reviewer can judge it; 'criterion' names the rubric criterion in system/00-core/test_review-rubric.md that scripts/test_calibrate_reviewer.py expects the reviewer to flag). Each id is also listed in tests/rules.lock, so a case cannot quietly disappear. The human-readable record is workspace/feedback-log.md.

cases.text:
Company Brain is a prototype that no real team has run yet; its multi-user design has been exercised only by its test suite. Its privacy rests on shared-folder permissions and a person's yes, and the yes is enforced by convention: Claude works with the person's own access, so it can technically approve anything they can. Human approval is a sound control, but only as one layer, since frequent prompts get approved by reflex.

In an enterprise, data owners decide who may see what, and IT and security enforce it in the identity provider and in the systems that hold the data. A real deployment would add single sign-on and provisioning, agents with their own scoped and short-lived credentials, authorization checked where the data lives, permissions that follow content into summaries and search, sensitivity labels and private areas, an audit trail of who approved what, and retention and residency rules.
